title: Six-month-olds can tell monkey faces apart; nine-month-olds can’t
body: Babies start out as perceptual generalists. In one study, six-month-olds familiarised with individual monkeys could tell the faces apart; retested at nine months, they no longer could, unless each monkey had been given a name, in which case the skill survived. This **perceptual narrowing** shows up with human faces too: young infants recognise faces across ethnic groups, but by nine months recognition works only within their own. The brain tunes itself to what it meets often, sharpening those perceptions at the cost of what it rarely meets.

left.label: 6 months
left.text: Tells individual monkey faces apart, and recognises faces from other ethnic groups.

right.label: 9 months
right.text: Monkey faces blur together, unless each monkey had a name. Face recognition now works only within the baby’s own group.

slides.heading: Tuning in to speech
items: Under 6 months: phonemes of different languages sound distinct
6 to 8 months: better than 8-to-10-month-olds at non-native sound contrasts
The narrowing leans heavily on social interaction, not just hearing sounds

slides.heading: Why narrow at all?
slides.text: Narrowing is not so much a loss as a specialisation: it sharpens perception of the faces and sounds a child actually lives among. Plasticity lasts a lifetime but is strongest early, which is why a label, a name or a conversation at the right moment can keep a door open.

slides.question: What kept the nine-month-olds able to tell the monkey faces apart?
options: Each monkey had been given a name
The faces were shown in colour
The faces were shown upside down
slides.explanation: Infants who had learned the monkeys with name labels still discriminated them at nine months; those who saw the faces without labels did not.
